Heimdall

Heimdall is a tool designed for concept drift detection in continuous data streams. When analyzing time series data, it is possible to observe significant changes in the data distribution or in the accuracy of predictive models during the forecasting process. These changes are known as concept drift.

The goal of the Heimdall package is to detect when concept drift occurs, enabling the detection and adaptation of models in non-stationary contexts. The package offers several state-of-the-art methods to identify and handle concept drift, as well as techniques for efficient model adaptation.

Heimdall is particularly useful when you need to move quickly from the theory of concept drift to a working streaming implementation. The package includes detectors for both real concept drift and virtual concept drift, and the repository examples are designed to help users understand that distinction through small, reproducible workflows.

Getting started

The package ships with three vignettes, also available on the package website:

  • vignette("heimdall") introduces the streaming workflow shared by every detector and shows how to monitor real and virtual concept drift;
  • vignette("adaptive-models") shows how stealthy() retrains a model automatically when a drift is detected;
  • vignette("configuring-detectors") shows how to read drifter_output, calibrate a threshold for your data, and choose between sliding and anchored windows.

Drifter outputs

Besides the drift decision, every drifter exposes the statistic it monitors. After fit(), obj$drifter_output is a data frame with one row per observation, and obj$last_drifter_output holds the value for the last observation processed by update_state(). Rows are NA when the detector reported nothing for that observation, for example while its window is still filling or when it skipped a missing value.

stealthy() exposes the output of its drifter in obj$drifter_output as well, with one row per row of x across every call to fit(). Rows are NA while the drifter is not monitoring (during the warmup, or after a drift until the model is retrained).

Drifter Type drifter_output columns
dfr_ddm() error-based miss_prob: running error rate
dfr_eddm() error-based mean_distance: mean distance between two consecutive errors
dfr_hddm() error-based estimation: running error rate
dfr_ecdd() error-based Z: exponentially weighted moving average of the errors
dfr_cusum() error-based g: cumulative sum compared with lambda
dfr_adwin() univariate width: current length of the adaptive window
dfr_page_hinkley() univariate ph_statistic: Page-Hinkley statistic compared with threshold (the larger of the two directions when direction = "both")
dfr_kswin() univariate D: Kolmogorov-Smirnov statistic; p: its p-value
dfr_lbdd() univariate levene_p: p-value of Levene’s test
dfr_mcdd() univariate old_shapiro_p, new_shapiro_p: normality p-values of the reference and recent halves; comparison_p: p-value of the t-test or Wilcoxon test
dfr_kldist() multivariate divergence: divergence between the reference and recent halves, compared with threshold
dfr_aedd() multivariate one column per feature: reconstruction error of the most recent row (encoder-decoder), or its encoding (encoder only)
dfr_multi_criteria() combined one logical column per drifter in drifter_list, with its decision on that observation
dfr_inactive(), dfr_passive() baseline no columns: they monitor nothing

Choosing what a detector monitors

Every distribution-based detector selects its input through target_feat:

  • univariate detectors (dfr_adwin(), dfr_page_hinkley(), dfr_kswin(), dfr_lbdd(), dfr_mcdd()) take a single column name;
  • multivariate detectors (dfr_kldist(), dfr_aedd()) take one or more column names, and monitor every numeric column when target_feat is NULL.

Inside stealthy() and dfr_multi_criteria(), a univariate detector without a target_feat receives the mean of each row. In stealthy(), column names refer to the one-hot encoded, normalized columns, so numeric columns keep their names.

What each detector cannot see

Each detector is blind to some kinds of change. Combine detectors with dfr_multi_criteria() when several kinds of change matter.

Drifter Reacts to Does not see
dfr_ddm(), dfr_hddm() increases of the error rate decreases of the error rate, and any change that leaves the error rate unchanged
dfr_eddm() errors becoming closer together changes that do not affect the distance between errors
dfr_ecdd(), dfr_cusum() increases of the error rate decreases of the error rate
dfr_page_hinkley() increases of the mean (decreases or both with direction) changes of spread or shape with the same mean
dfr_adwin() changes of the mean changes of spread or shape with the same mean
dfr_mcdd() changes of location (mean or median) changes of spread with the same centre
dfr_lbdd() changes of spread shifts of the mean with the same spread
dfr_kswin() any change of the distribution of one feature changes in the relation between features
dfr_kldist() changes of the marginal distribution of each feature; with the default 100-row window, shifts of about two standard deviations small shifts (below about one standard deviation with the default window) and changes in the relation between features
dfr_aedd() changes of the joint distribution, through the reconstruction error changes that the autoencoder reconstructs equally well

Distribution-based detectors only see virtual concept drift (changes in the inputs); error-based detectors only see real concept drift that degrades the predictions.

Long streams

  • The window-based detectors (dfr_kswin(), dfr_lbdd(), dfr_mcdd(), dfr_kldist(), dfr_aedd()) run a statistical test or a comparison at every evaluation. monitoring_step is the main speed control: with monitoring_step = 10, the test runs once every ten observations.
  • stealthy(history_size = ) bounds the rows kept in drifter_output and drifter_input.
  • nrm_memory(max_size = ) bounds the history used to estimate the normalization.

Examples

Heimdall usage examples are organized to help users learn the package progressively, not only to list detector names. Every drifter has two examples:

  • a detection example, where the detector monitors a stream on its own through the update_state() loop;
  • an online prediction example, where the detector is plugged into stealthy() to retrain a classifier whenever a drift is reported.

Each example is available as a rendered walkthrough, an extracted R script and a Word document.

Recommended starting points:

  • dfr_adwin for a simple univariate distribution-monitoring example;
  • dfr_ddm for an error-based supervised example;
  • dfr_aedd for a multivariate unsupervised example;
  • dfr_inactive and dfr_passive as baselines to compare any detector against.

Browse the materials here:

  • Examples directory

Installation

The latest version of Heimdall is available on CRAN:

install.packages("heimdall")

You can install the development version directly from GitHub:

# install.packages("devtools")
library(devtools)
devtools::install_github("cefet-rj-dal/heimdall", force = TRUE, upgrade = "never")
